author: Brian Lund
title: Arizona's minimum wage is expected to rise 50 cents to $15.65 an hour in January under the state's inflation formula - NewsBreak
text:
By Brian Lund ,
1 days ago
Arizona’s next minimum-wage adjustment is not yet official, but the arithmetic behind it is public. Under a formula written into state law, the Industrial Commission of Arizona raises the wage floor every January by the percentage the Consumer Price Index rose over the prior August-to-August period, then rounds the result to the nearest five cents. Applying that formula to the 3.4 percent inflation reading reported for the year ending in August 2026 points to a new hourly minimum of $15.65, a 50-cent increase from the $15.15 rate that has applied since the start of 2026. The commission has not yet posted a formal 2027 notice, so the figure remains a projection rather than a published rate.
How the Industrial Commission of Arizona Sets the January Rate Arizona voters created the annual adjustment in 2016 by approving Proposition 206, the Fair Wages and Healthy Families Act, which now lives in Arizona Revised Statutes Section 23-363(B). The commission’s own 2026 rate notice shows how the statute works in practice: it set the current $15.15-an-hour floor, effective January 1, 2026, as a 45-cent increase over the prior year’s $14.70, based on “the increase in inflation between August 2024 and August 2025, as published in the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Consumer Price Index.”
The commission’s frequently-asked-questions guide describes the mechanism plainly: the rate “is evaluated annually based on the increase in the cost of living,” and any “statutory adjustments are implemented at the beginning of the calendar year.” No commission vote, ballot measure or legislative session is required for the number to move; the formula alone determines it once the relevant Consumer Price Index reading is final.
What a raise does not fix: A higher hourly rate changes what arrives in a paycheck, not what a checking account already owes to an overdraft cycle or an old collections balance, and the two-month window that shields certain deposits from a garnishment order runs on its own separate clock. What the 3.4 Percent Inflation Reading Produces KTAR.com, a Phoenix-area news outlet, ran the commission’s own formula against the latest inflation data and reported that the Consumer Price Index rose 3.4 percent between August 2025 and August 2026. Multiplying the current $15.15 rate by that increase produces roughly $15.665 an hour, and the statute’s five-cent rounding rule turns that into a clean $15.65, exactly 50 cents above today’s floor. That is the same rounding step the commission used a year earlier to arrive at $15.15 from $14.70.
The outlet tied part of the year’s inflation reading to higher gasoline prices, though the Consumer Price Index feeding the formula covers a broad basket of goods and services rather than fuel costs alone.
Why the Number Is Still Only “Expected” Last year’s cycle offers the clearest guide to timing: the commission’s press release setting the $15.15 rate for 2026 is dated September 29, 2025, roughly two weeks after the relevant August Consumer Price Index data became available. A similar release for 2027 had not yet appeared on the commission’s site as of September 25, 2026, which is why $15.65 is described as an expected result of the formula rather than an announced rate. Once the notice is issued, it typically arrives alongside an updated workplace poster that employers must display.
How This Year’s Increase Compares With Last Year’s The commission’s own numbers show the raise moving in a narrow band from one year to the next. The rate rose 45 cents, from $14.70 to $15.15, between 2025 and 2026, a jump that works out to roughly a 3.1 percent increase. The formula’s expected outcome for 2027 is a slightly larger 50-cent step, to $15.65, driven by the higher 3.4 percent Consumer Price Index reading for the year ending in August 2026. Both increases come from the identical calculation in Arizona Revised Statutes Section 23-363(B); the only variable that changes from year to year is how much inflation the index recorded over the preceding twelve months.
What a 50-Cent Raise Would Change on a Weekly Paycheck For a worker earning the state minimum on a standard 40-hour week, the difference between $15.15 and $15.65 an hour comes to $20 more before taxes each week, or roughly $1,040 across a full year of full-time hours. A worker logging fewer hours, such as 25 a week, would see the raise add about $12.50 a week, or roughly $650 over a year. Either way, the increase applies before any withholding for taxes, insurance or retirement contributions is subtracted. Multiplied across a two-income household in which both workers earn the state minimum, the same 50-cent increase would add roughly $2,080 to combined annual pay before taxes, assuming both put in a standard 40-hour week.
How Employers and Workers Learn the Final Rate Arizona law puts responsibility for publicizing the new number on the commission itself rather than on individual employers. The commission’s labor and minimum-wage page hosts each year’s poster, which businesses statewide are required to display once a new rate takes effect. A worker who wants to confirm the 2027 number once it becomes official can check that same page rather than relying on a projected figure. If the commission’s 2027 release follows last year’s late-September timing, the formal notice and its accompanying poster would likely appear within days of this report’s publication, well ahead of the rate’s January 1 effective date.
summary: Under a formula written into state law, the Industrial Commission of Arizona raises the wage floor every January by the percentage the Consumer Price Index rose over the prior August-to-August period, then rounds the result to the nearest five cents. What a raise does not fix: A higher hourly rate changes what arrives in a paycheck, not what a checking account already owes to an overdraft cycle or an old collections balance, and the two-month window that shields certain deposits from a garnishment order runs on its own separate clock.
